In a recent development, change has always been the fundamental operational signal in infrastructure. Empirik is turning that signal into the foundation for autonomous, agentic infrastructure engineering.

Change has always been the fundamental operational signal in infrastructure. Empirik is turning that signal into the foundation for autonomous, agentic infrastructure engineering.

Sources indicate that this one started close to home. Before Sequoia, our Chief Digital and Information Officer, Avon Puri, had spent two decades running IT and infrastructure at scale as SVP & CIO at Rubrik, and VP of Engineering and Applications at VMware (also my alma mater in the tech world). Avon and Sudheer Dhurjati, who worked alongside him at all three companies, watched the same story repeat: enterprise infrastructure operates in a reactive posture. Companies spend tens of billions of dollars on observabilityâmetrics, logs, and tracesâto tell us when a system is failing. But traditional observability is inherently post-mortem.

The real driver of infrastructure behavior is change: a new identity policy is attached, a new Terraform provider completes, or a feature flag flips in production. However, change has been treated as an administrative process constraint, a static ticket, an approval form, or as tribal knowledge buried in email or Slack. It was sometimes recorded for compliance, but never truly put to work to do actual infrastructure engineering jobs.

In a recent development, if you understand the real-time stream of changes across every layer of the environment, you don't just get better alertsâyou unlock true autonomy. Every change reflects an engineer's intent; once a system can interpret that intent and assess its impact, it can decide whether to act on its own or loop in a human. By bringing agentic capabilities to infrastructure, you solve the full lifecycle of infrastructure engineering jobs, shifting from a reactive firefighting posture to a proactive one.

Sources indicate that that insight became the founding pillar behind Empirik. Avon and Sudheer built the initial version inside Sequoia. We saw companies rushing to deploy AI agents to automate coding, marketing, and many other enterprise processes, but infrastructure was the one place nobody was modernizing. After the same rigorous evaluation any other Sequoia investment goes through, Empirik spun out as an independent company. And now, itâs under the leadership of CEO Kartik Chandrayana, a repeat founder who sold his first company, Twin Prime, to Salesforce, then spent five years as Salesforce's VP of Product for Observability and Big Data, and most recently was CPO at Quantum Metric. Today, we're excited to share that Empirik is emerging from stealth with $21M in funding.

Recent findings suggest that agentic coding has taken off because code lives in version-controlled repositories that make a system's architecture and intent legible to a model. Infrastructure has never had that foundation. Infrastructure-as-code is a good start, but because it represents a declared state and not what's actually running in production, it's inherently behind. There's no unified, real-time representation of an organization's infrastructure across the maze of cloud resources, Kubernetes, networking, identity, and legacy systems. Infrastructure does not have the notion of a pull request; instead, every change still runs through tribal knowledge and institutional memory of people rather than the machine rigor of software.

According to recent reports, observability is already a large, proven marketâDatadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk are behemoths with billions in revenue. But all of observability is built to measure symptoms: latency spiked, errors climbed, a pod crashed. Empirik's bet is that there's a fourth pillar hiding in plain sightâthe changes themselves. Instead of "latency in service X increased 300% in the last 24 hours," Empirik tells you, "Joe deployed a Terraform provider that shut down three VMs in AWS"âthe actual cause and context, not just the symptom. And why stop there? With Empirik, you can actually warn or stop Joe even before he deploys Terraform because Empirik computes that risk at the inception of change.

As Kartik describes it: infrastructure today is where software engineering was three years agoâbefore Claude Code and Cursor, when every action needed a human in the loop because there was no reliable map of the system to reason over. Empirik is building that map, and putting it to work as the Autonomous Infra EngineerâAI that can safely plan, reason about, and operate enterprise infrastructure. It's already plugged into agentic workflows via MCP, connecting directly into tools like Claude and ChatGPT, so that humans and agents alike can reason over infrastructure change with real contextânot guesswork.

Industry observers note that under the hood is an infrastructure compiler. Just as a traditional compiler translates source code into executable software, Empirik converts metadata from a customerâs clouds, identity providers, CI/CD, and SaaS systems into a live, unified operational graphâmapping thousands of relationships between assets and accounts. That graph is how the product knows, in real time, what changed, who changed it, and whether itâs the reason something broke.

What I particularly appreciate about the teamâs approach is that they didnât take shortcuts. Itâs easy for modern startups to build exclusively for greenfield Kubernetes or a single public cloud provider. But from day one, Avon, Sudheer, and Kartik designed Empirik for the reality of the Fortune 500 enterprise: a complex, multi-decade hybrid stack spanning public clouds, legacy on-prem infrastructure, identity layers, and critical SaaS apps. An infrastructure graph that only sees half your environment misses the mark for an enterprise buyer. Empirikâs graph connects the entire surface area so teams and agents have complete operational context.

In a recent development, the traction backs up the thesis. Fortune500 Financial enterpriseâs interest in the product traces directly back to a P0 outage caused by an unapproved change. TCBPay, a payment processing organization with $1.5B+ in annual volume now catches sensitive config file changes in 10 seconds, down from 30 minutes. Avahi, an MSP, integrated Empirik within their GitHub Actions to evaluate and block risky changes at the source. Guardant Health found Empirik so valuable that it expanded its deployment from production to all dev environments, and even expanded to on-prem. And a global Fortune-50 CPG company is also expanding its footprint, relying on Empirik to drive most of its agentic and autonomous infra roadmap. Empirik is now processing millions of raw change and telemetry events every week, over dependency graphs spanning a few million resources across all major clouds and on-prem systems. Customers are reporting benefits in multiple domains: preventing risky changes from making it to production, detecting unapproved changes, faster incident response, making rollback decisions, and detecting drifts, among others.

The success is no surprise given this team. Avon and Sudheer are two of the best operators we know, and they built Empirik the way they'd have wanted it built for themselves. Kartik, meanwhile, has firsthand expertise in shipping observability products at enterprise scale. Most enterprises still can't answer that simple but critical question: what changed, and did that cause the incident? Empirik is building the system of record for that questionâfor humans today, and for the agents that will increasingly be making those changes themselves tomorrow.

By Bogomil Balkansky, Dean Meyer and David Cahn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every agent now imports plugins and skills from random places. Yair and Niv are building the software supply chain defenses for AI.

In a recent development, every agent now imports plugins and skills from random places. Yair and Niv are building the software supply chain defenses for AI.

We met Yair Saban and Niv Hoffman before they had a company, a name, or a product. But as we ran our references on them across the Israeli cybersecurity ecosystem, the same answer kept coming back: they would be among the strongest founding teams in the country. One of the former commanders of Unit 8200 told us Yair was "the only person I have ever thought had everything required to one day command Unit 8200" â about as strong an endorsement as exists in Israeli tech. Niv is a technical outlier who led 8200âs most important vulnerability research department, building a network of elite technical talent. Yair finished his service on a Thursday, and we shook hands on a seed investment that Saturday, which tells you all you need to know about the pace at which this team operates.

Recent findings suggest that well before Yair and Niv started building a defensive security product, they built MOAK, the "Mother of All KEVs," an agentic workflow that produces working exploits for freshly published vulnerabilities with no human in the loop. In one demonstration, MOAK exploited a React vulnerability in 21 minutes, versus the six days or so it takes a typical enterprise to roll out a patch. They released it publicly, to ring an alarm bell that the industry was badly underestimating the leverage attackers can now get from AI, and that defensive tooling needed to catch up.

Sources indicate that the day developers started importing other people's packages instead of writing everything themselves, software acquired a supply chain. It then took two decades and a number of painful incidents, from log4j to Solarwinds, to build the machinery for inspecting what was coming in. Agents now have precisely the same problem, except that their supply chain is assembled at runtime and often nobody is inspecting it at all. An enterprise agent consumes skills, plugins, MCP servers, sub-agents, hooks, commands and rules â each running with the agentâs own permissions, inside a userâs environment, against a userâs data. Usually, theyâre installed with the care most of us would give a browser extension.

Industry observers note that air has spent the past several months demonstrating the stakes. They wrote a deliberately malicious skill and watched multiple AI marketplaces wave it through as safe. Their Story of Skills research indicated a researcher-built malicious skill reaching more than 26,000 agents through a trusted marketplace and social media, with every scanner clearing it. Then they published SkillJacking, which showed 925 live skills were pulling their dependencies and prompts from dead links; Air registered those links and took control of the roughly 134,000 agents that had installed them. Every public scanner they tested missed the problems completely.

It has been revealed that the same day, Yair and Niv shipped ScanAir, an OWASP-aligned scanner for agentic skills. That sequence â find the hole, prove it, publish it, then ship the thing that closes it â is the pattern we like most about this team.

In a recent development, today, Air has three products that between them cover the full lifecycle of an agent's add-ons. Air Filter vets every add-on before an agent is permitted to consume it, using static analysis, dependency checks and sandbox detonation. It then intercepts unsafe installations in real time and offers safe alternatives in their place. Air Defend monitors what agents actually do once theyâre running and provides security operations teams with detection and response capabilities for agent behavior. Finally, Air Control handles posture and policy, from knowing which agents exist and what theyâre allowed to touch, to revoking a bad skill across thousands of agents at once. Think of it like home security: Air Filter is the locks and the childproofing, Air Defend is the cameras and the person watching them, and Air Control is the panel by the door â every entry point accounted for, every code assigned, and all of them revocable at once.

In a recent development, every couple of years, the best cyber talent coming out of Unit 8200 consolidates around a handful of teams. First it was Wiz, Cyera, and, Island; then it was Eon, Glow, Decart, and Kela; now it is Air. Yair and Niv are smart, hungry natural leaders who have proven their ability to attract extreme talent density; in only a few short months they have built a cracked team of the very best. We at Sequoia are proud to led their seed round, and to now double down in their Series A.

As enterprises move toward handing agents real authority over real systems, every CISO will be asked the same questions: what is our agent actually running, where did it come from, and who checked it? Today, few have complete answers. But Air is building the system of record that will.

Tech Report: The Cognitive Revolution

📅 02 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We externalized our muscles and built the modern world.
  • Sources indicate that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world.
  • The car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Sources indicate that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Most mornings I ride to work in a Waymo.

The car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area. The car is also doing cognitive work: reading the road and making predictions that result in 17x fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers.

Recent findings suggest that the experience asks nothing of my muscles and nothing of my mind. Both have been externalized.

In a recent development, this one ride encapsulates two revolutions. The physical one is 200 years old. The cognitive one has barely started.

It seems the mood around that second revolution is a cocktail of optimism, skepticism and anxiety. Talk of a singularity. Recursive self-improvement. Trillion-dollar clusters. Superintelligence. Unemployment. Social disruption. A race between superpowers. Itâs dizzying.

My view is far from dizzying. I think we have already undergone a transition that rhymes with the AI revolution in the coming decades: the Industrial Revolution.

Sources indicate that we can bifurcate work into physical work and cognitive work. Most valuable tasks necessitate both.

It has been revealed that agriculture is one of the oldest examples. Working the land took muscle, ours and our animals', for ten thousand years. It also took insight: reading the seasons, observing which seed produced which yield, etc.

Sources indicate that the two kinds of work are different. Physical work is force times distance: moving mass through space. Cognitive work is thinking. But both are scarce, have a price, and get applied to a task somebody wants done. In both cases when price collapses, supply floods in. In most cases, demand expands to meet supply.

According to recent reports, for most of history, nearly all physical work done for humans was done by muscle, ours and animals. The chart above goes flat before the 1700s, and the flat part runs back as far as we do.

In the late 1700s and early 1800s things started to change. First steam, then combustion and the electric motor. Each wave took a larger share of the world's physical work. Over the course of about two centuries, physical work went from 99% biological to 99.9% machine.

Today the results are everywhere. The screen youâre reading this on. Nearly every article of clothing youâre wearing. The plane that carried you on your last trip. The lattice of ships, trains and trucks behind every ordinary product in modern life. Human muscle is a rounding error in the global energy budget.

For most of history, essentially all cognitive work was done by humans (plus a small assist from animals like the sheepdog). On top of that sat a thin mechanical sliver: tools that computed a little, like the clock or Pascal's mechanical calculator.

Then came electronic computation. Inside a century, it spread from simple calculations and spreadsheets to trillions then quadrillions of operations running 24 hours per day. Navigating your commute, processing payroll, pricing your insuranceâ¦this is all cognitive work done by machines.

According to recent reports, the next wave is neural networks. This wave drastically expands the types of cognitive work machines can do. Just as combustion engines magnified the scope of the Industrial Revolution, neural networks are set to accelerate the Cognitive Revolution.

It has been revealed that A century ago, 99% of cognitive work was done by humans. In the near future, 99.9% will be done by machines. Not because humans will think less, but because machines will compute much much more.

The parallel in the two curves is stark. The Cognitive Revolution will look a lot like the Industrial Revolution. But it will be bigger and much faster. Divide the global economy by the nature of work, and cognitive and physical work could split a ~$120 trillion world economy roughly equally. The physical half has been mechanizing for 200 years. The cognitive half has barely started.

It has been revealed that so what actually happens in a revolution like this? Letâs run it back.

It has been revealed that the industrial age required massively scaling up input commodities: first coal and iron, then oil and steel. Iron was made by a process known as puddling. Steel was made by a process called the Bessemer process.

The parallel is clear: electricity and compute. The âprocessâ here are algorithms like the Transformer.

The providers of those components were the titans of their era. Carnegie and U.S. Steel, Rockefeller and Standard Oil. Process designers like Henry Bessemer. The modern equivalents are Jensen Huang's NVIDIA, Morris Changâs TSMC, authors of the Transformer paper, founders of the great Model Labs and the hyperscalers pouring trillions into data centers. Nations that once measured power in refining capacity will measure it in grid capacity and intelligence output.

According to recent reports, A unit of mechanical work in 1900 cost a small fraction of what it cost in 1800. That collapse in price made mass production possible, and made the revolution universal rather than a curiosity for the rich.

Recent findings suggest that the cost of cognition is collapsing faster. Intelligence per Watt has been falling more than 10x per year.

With price decline, customers will buy wildly, absurdly more intelligence.

It has been revealed that nobody in 1800 flew to Tokyo, shipped strawberries across a hemisphere in January, or air-conditioned Phoenix. All these are physical processes that either were impossible or impractically expensive.

It has been revealed that demand for physical work exploded once upcoming technologies were invented and price collapsed. William Jevons identified the phenomenon in 1865: more efficient engines did not reduce Britain's coal consumption. They multiplied it.

Industry observers note that cognition will follow the same pattern, and here the latent demand is almost unbounded in scale. Most problems on Earth currently go un-thought-about, because thinking is expensive. A doctor has limited time and doesnât review the latest literature. A radiologist studies a scan for minutes instead of hours. A small business owner has no budget for a financial analyst.

When cognition costs approach zero, every curiosity can get a research team.

In a recent development, the amount of thinking done by machines will grow by orders of magnitude. Which raises the question, what will all that thinking be spent on?

The primal application of the Industrial Revolution was spinning textiles.

Sources indicate that spinning and weaving were skilled work. Textile makers were respected in your society: years of apprenticeship, a craft guild, a trade the family had held for generations. In 1764, James Hargreaves built the Spinning Jenny, which let one person spin eight threads at once, and later eighty. Clothing prices fell rapidly and global clothing consumption exploded.

Recent findings suggest that the big change was the human moving from performing the task to supervising it. One person tending a frame produced what a room of hand-spinners once had.

It has been revealed that the primal skilled application of this era is AI coding. Writing software is our era's elite craft: highly skilled, highly paid, a decade to master. And it is the first cognitive task where the pattern has fully flipped. The machine now completes most of the work, and the engineer's job is to direct, review and correct it. Itâs no accident that this is where the Cognitive Revolution found its first commercial traction.

While textiles kicked off the industrial revolution, they did not define it. The ultimate innovation of the industrial revolution was the automobile: a civilization grew around it, including suburbs, highways, supply chains, and the entire geography of modern life.

Coding agents are our Spinning Jennies: the first act, automating a skilled cognitive task. The automobile of this revolution has probably not been built yet. It will be something that was impossible while thinking was scarce.

My candidates: science conducted at machine speed, the personal agent that serves your life the way a chief of staff organizes a CEO's, or something in how humans connect and coordinate. In 1800, the automobile would have been hard to predict.

In a recent development, in 1800, over 75% of American workers worked the land. Machines came for that work. Today, farming is about 1% of U.S. employment. By the pessimists' arithmetic, over 74% of the country should be unemployed.

Sources indicate that instead we invented work no farmer in 1800 could have named. Radiologist. Software engineer. Podcast producer. Flight attendant. The machines did not end labor. They eliminated categories of work and expanded the total amount of it. There are more people employed today than at any point in human history, and they are vastly richer than their ancestors. All of my ancestors worked in agriculture 100 years ago. I knew all four of my grandparents, all of whom were born to farming families. None of them finished their lives in agriculture. All of them considered the non-agricultural work they did at the end of their lives more pleasant and prosperous than the hard agricultural work their families had done for generations.

In a recent development, the same is taking shape in the Cognitive revolution. Despite the âspinning Jennyâ phenomena in AI coding, data supports that demand for software engineers, the most AI exposed occupation was accelerating higher, has inflected. In the coming week, we plan to share data supporting inflections in hiring in other areas being transformed by AI, including Legal Services and Financial Services.

Machines doing cognitive work will not mean humans stop doing cognitive work any more than the tractor meant humans stopped doing physical things. The specific tasks change. The junior analyst who builds the model by hand becomes the person directing a hundred models. Further, categories of work we cannot presently name will grow the way "engineer" became a job following the invention of the engine during the Industrial Revolution.

Recent findings suggest that like in the industrial revolution, the aggregate story will be triumphant. But, the individual story will frequently not be. The handloom weavers of Lancashire were not retrained into locomotive engineers. Many of them simply lost, and their losses spanned a generation. The economic historian Robert Allen gave the period a name: Engels' pause. Between 1780 and 1840, British output per worker rose 46%. Real wages rose 12%.

According to recent reports, luddites were not wrong about their own lives, but about their childrenâs and grandchildren's. Between 1840 and 1900, British output per worker rose 90% and real wages rose 123%. Wages caught up to productivity, and then outran it.

Sources indicate that A pause is not a foregone conclusion. Mark Zuckerberg put this well recently: âThere is no rule that AI must increase automation faster than it increases individuals' capabilities or demand for new skills.â Humanityâs demand for new skills, for better and worse, will be insatiable.The difference this time is speed. The Industrial Revolution gave a farmhand's son forty years to become a factory hand. This revolution may offer five. Society's shock absorbers, like education, retraining, and safety nets, were designed for the old clock. The central policy question of the next two decades is whether we can help humans transform as fast as the jobs do.

The Industrial Revolution created the modern education system, in at least two ways.

First, it made mass education possible. When most of humanity had to work the fields, children were labor. Machines taking over the physical work is what freed children to sit in classrooms and freed societies to fund them. The modern university exists because society no longer needed every able body in the field, and could redirect a civilization's youth toward cognitive skill-building instead.

According to recent reports, second, and less flatteringly, it shaped what education became. The factory needed workers who could read instructions, do arithmetic, show up on time and perform standardized tasks in synchronized shifts. So we built schools that look suspiciously like factories: Bells. Rows. Fixed schedules. Batch processing by age. Standardized outputs. Mass education was, in large part, industrial job training.

It has been revealed that the Cognitive Revolution upends both of these dynamics. If machines do the cognition, the factory-model school is the equivalent of training for hand-spinning. But the deeper change is on the delivery side. For all of history, the binding constraint on education was the ratio of teachers to students. Benjamin Bloom quantified the cost of that constraint in 1984: the average student tutored one-to-one with mastery learning outperformed 98% of students in a conventional classroom.

That constraint is dissolving. The marginal cost of an infinitely patient, endlessly knowledgeable tutor is approaching zero. Hybrid human-AI tutors are found to be more effective and less costly than traditional education. Further, new hybrid AI approaches could help spread education in parts of the world where public education has been prohibitively expensive.

Industry observers note that modern medicine was also built by the industrial revolution. Mass production gave us penicillin at scale, refrigeration that made vaccines deliverable, and the chemical industry that spawned the pharmaceutical industry.

It has been revealed that the Cognitive Revolution pushes this much further. Drug discovery is a search across a space too large for humans to comprehend, which is exactly the work that scales best when cognition gets cheap. By predicting structures for virtually every known protein, AlphaFold solved a challenge where even minor breakthroughs previously demanded entire lifelong careers.Thousands of diseases currently have no treatment, not because they are unsolvable but because the cost of investigating each was never justified by the number of patients. When that cost collapses, the long tail becomes addressable the way every other latent demand does.

According to recent reports, curing disease has been the ambition of every generation of physicians. This is the first generation where the binding constraint is no longer how many of them there are.

Then there are the doctors in clinical practice. We face a massive shortage of physicians both in the United States and globally, with demand far exceeding supply. This issue is deeply personal to me, as I have long seen healthcare workers in my family stretched thin attempting to meet patient needs. Cheaper, accessible cognitive tools will not lead to doctors taking time off; instead, they will allow more patients to receive higher-quality care. Given the virtually limitless demand for better healthcare, scalable intelligence can help shift our medical model from reactive treatment to proactive care.The Shape of Daily Life.

It has been revealed that beyond work and school, the Industrial Revolution changed the texture of ordinary life so thoroughly that we now mistake its artifacts for human nature. The Cognitive Revolution will change them once again.

In a recent development, clock time. Before factories, rural work followed seasons and sunlight. But a factory owner needed hundreds of people to start and stop simultaneously. The machine ran on a schedule, so the humans had to. Rigid shifts, the workday, the work week, modern timekeeping itself: these are industrial inventions, barely two centuries old. The Cognitive Revolution loosens their grip. When your machine colleagues work continuously and asynchronously, there is no reason for a hundred humans to think in unison from nine to five. Work drifts back toward task rhythms rather than clock rhythms.

Home and Work. Work happened in and around the home for most of human history: the farm, the cottage workshop, the family trade. Industrialization pulled the workplace out of domestic space because the work had to happen where the machine was. The daily commute is the residue of that separation. The Cognitive Revolution reverses it, because the machine now lives everywhere and one of the most powerful tools in history fits in your pocket. Home and work are recombining.

Recent findings suggest that global trade and power. Industrial nations imported raw materials and exported finished goods, an asymmetry that drove imperialism. The upcoming raw materials are energy, compute and algorithms. The finished good is intelligence. The last time this asymmetry appeared, it defined a century of international order and disorder: the same industrial base that laid rail and poured steel also eventually created atomic bombs. Intelligence will be dual-use in the same way, and faster. The Industrial Revolution lifted humanity, but its safeguards arrived late. This time we should try to be earlier.

Follow the thread and you eventually arrive at the real question underneath the anxiety about AI: If the machines do the thinking, what are we for?

The last revolution already answered the physical version. At the end of the Industrial Revolution, humans did not stop moving their bodies. We remained embodied creatures.

Industry observers note that proportionally, fewer of us work intense physical jobs. However, far more of us move for sport and purpose: we run marathons, climb mountains, and pay for the privilege of holding yoga poses in uncomfortably hot rooms. Along the way, we created sports-leagues and even the modern Olympics were the result of the Industrial Revolution.

Sources indicate that cognition will make the same migration. Chess is a clean example. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 and Kasparov later half-jokingly described himself as the first knowledge worker whose job was threatened by a machine. Chess did not die. More people play it today than at any point in history. When AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, researchers found that the novelty of moves played by human Go professionals increased significantly afterward. Superhuman machines made human play more creative, not less. The âcentaurâ era of machine-human collaboration was brief, but the human era never ended.

It has been revealed that critics of this essay will argue that âthis time is different.â Specifically, they will point out that humans were the smartest animals on earth and that this is the first time something uniquely human is displaced by a machine. That is incorrect. It is incorrect for at least two reasons. First, thinking is not uniquely human. Animals think. Even nature follows complex and âintelligentâ patterns. Second, there are many uniquely human skills that machines exceed already. For example, making fire is strictly a human skillâ¦and now your stove does it with the press of a button. Same with writing and transferring information (the internet). Same with making tools (us and chimpanzees), but now machines make most of our tools. And then Einstein reinvented it completely-- humans making a comeback -- with a latest human thought experiment that was needed to accurately plot the orbit of Mercury! Flight was a super-human task until airplanes made it accessible. This time is different, but not that different.What stays economically human the longest is what was never really cognition to begin with: wanting things, choosing between them, being accountable for the choice, and being trusted by other people. The machine can draft the treaty. Someone still has to sign it. Over 2500 years ago, Greek philosopher Protagaros wrote "Man is the measure of all things." Indeed, value as we experience it is in what we offer to other people.

Stand far enough back and this is all one story. For all of history, humans did the work: with our muscles and with our minds. Twice, we built machines that took the work and externalized it to machines.

The first time, we were terrified, and the fear was short-term justified and long-term wrong. The world after the machines took most of the physical work was profoundly more abundant, healthy  and humane.

It has been revealed that the same trade is on the table now, at greater scale and higher speed. The Cognitive Revolution will be turbulent, unevenly distributed, and deeply uncomfortable . And, it will end the way the last one did: with the world unrecognizably better, its results so completely woven into daily life that our grandchildren will live inside them.

We have made this trip before.This time, we can navigate it with our eyes open: shaping the transition calmly, sharing the prosperity, and remembering that the goal of externalizing our minds is ultimately to elevate our humanity.

Industry observers note that controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

Controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

Every large enterprise now has an AI mandate. Very few know exactly what happens when an agent is granted access to enterprise systems and data. What exactly will it be able to reach? How will we know what it did with it? These questions â not model quality, not cost, not talent â are the reason so many enterprise AI programs stay stuck in pilots. Cymphony was built to answer them.

Employees increasingly work together with AI agents to execute day-to-day work. But the typical agent is nothing like an employee. It can be provisioned in minutes rather than hired over weeks. It works continuously. And it can reach across far more systems, data, and capability than an individual person. Every one of those properties is what makes an AI agent worth deploying â and every one of them is what makes a security team say no.

Recent findings suggest that governance and security are already major barriers to AI adoption, with 40% of enterprises expected to demote or decommission autonomous AI agents over governance concerns by next year. That is not a prediction about AI failing to work. Itâs about enterprises pulling back working agents because they cannot see or control what those agents reaching. The fundamental challenge is not utility, but accountability.

Recent findings suggest that for decades, security teams have built tools around two separate concerns: where sensitive data lives, and who has access. The first produced the tools that watch files, inboxes, and databases for leaks. The second produced the identity industry. But both assume the "who"s are human employees.

Recent findings suggest that AI broke that assumption. An identity tool can tell you an agent exists. A data tool can tell you a file is sensitive. Neither can tell you that a given agent, acting on behalf of a given employee, can reach that file right now. Identity security and data security are no longer separable.

In a recent development, cymphony continuously maps both employees and agents across an enterprise, graphing who and what can reach which systems and information. It is a difficult engineering problem: the same person routinely holds a dozen different accounts scattered across systems that were never designed to talk to each other, and agents inherit access from the humans and applications that spawned them. Stitching all of that back into one accurate picture requires more than a dashboard that aggregates alerts.

Sources indicate that what we love about working with co-founders Shy Dekel, Idan Berkovits, and Edi Gotlieb is their instinct to build not for the alert but for the workflow. Instead of stopping at detection and leaving a security analyst to figure out what to do next, Cymphony pushes further â recommending and even automating remediation, and coordinating with the people who need to take action.

Enterprise customers including Syngenta, KKR, Cass Information Systems, and Athennian are already seeing results. Sequoia is also a happy customer. We are proud to have led Cymphonyâs seed round, and to now co-lead their Series A.

Sources indicate that we met Shy, Idan, and Edi through Sequoia's Israel network, introduced separately by two people in our orbit who each remarked some version of the same thing: these three had spent their careers on hard, unglamorous security problem many founders avoid, and they were building something different around it. All three came out of Israel's elite Talpiot program. All three have deep experience in this space: Shy led the cyber department for Unit 8200, Idan ran a research group in the Office of the Prime Minister and won an Israel Defense Prize, and Edi built hardware at Apple and at the Israeli Ministry of Defense. Every large enterprise software tech giant has been built on a transition: the underlying unit of work changes, and the old categories are no longer the right shape. Cloud changed where software ran, and security rebuilt itself around it. Mobile changed what an endpoint was, and it rebuilt itself again. Each time, the companies that offered visibility and control over what came next eventually became infrastructure everyone else took for granted.

AI is no exception, albeit the first shift where the fresh unit of work can act on its own. The tech giant that lets an enterprise say yes to agents â confidently, at scale, with a record of what they did â will be not just a feature inside the AI stack, but a precondition for it. We think Cymphony is building that layer, and we are glad to be part of it.

By Bogomil Balkansky, Dean Meyer and David Cahn.

For years, "using AI" has mostly meant humans typing into a box and waiting for an answer. The next chapter belongs to agents. Machines chase solutions to any problem with patience and tenacity, bound only by the compute and context they are given.

Industry observers note that the demand for agents is here. The infrastructure to run them ambitiously is not. Sail is the platform to run agents ambitiously.

Sail is building for a world in which agents run for hours or days to solve our most complex problems. Sail purpose-built their inference platform to operate across a wide range of compute and flex to handle long running, agent tasks. To make this happen, the Sail team is pushing on two key technologies:.

The first is their inference stack, the machinery that actually runs the models. Sail lives by a simple mantra, "there are no bad chips, only bad prices." The team took the inference stack apart and rebuilt it to squeeze far more out of every chip. They distribute work intelligently across providers so nothing stalls. They tap underused data-center capacity that would otherwise sit idle, particularly clusters too small or too old for anyone else to want. They're often among the first to try latest accelerators as they hit the market, always searching for a way to find a productive place for them in their engine.

This improved stack allows agents to think longer and harder, spending billions of tokens on a single task, for a fraction of the cost.

Recent findings suggest that the second is Sailboxes, the workspace for agents that want to run forever. Sailboxes fluidly scale CPU and memory to match the userâs needs, so an agent waiting on an event or long-running tool call is billed almost nothing for that time. Customers can and do leave Sailboxes running for months; theyâre basically immortal. Sailboxes underpin a wide range of customer use cases, from always-on security checks, monitoring every physical product on the web, and even powering a chess leaderboard that has been running for months at the Sail office.The Sail team isnât upcoming to the world of compute infrastructure. Neil Movva started his career at NVIDIA pushing GPUs to their limits, then did the same for new generations of AI accelerators at Apple, and came full circle back to GPUs at Together AI. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

AI took the digital world by storm in a few short years, and we are still only scratching the surface. Each time digital AI has moved to a upcoming phase, from pretraining to reinforcement learning to deployment, spend on compute and data has not plateaued. It has accelerated.

Bringing AI into the physical world will be a wave of comparable importance to digital AI, if not larger, but the infrastructure required to get there will be harder to build and scale, and that already reveals at every stage. In pretraining, language models benefited from decades of text accumulated on the internet. Robotics has no comparable, ready-made collection of the movements, interactions and sensory information needed to understand the physical world. That experience has to be captured before it can be learned from. In reinforcement learning and deployment, digital AI operates in clean, structured environments that are easy to scale. Physical AI lives in the noisy, unpredictable, operationally complex reality of the real world. It operates in the field, not in the cloud.

To reach physical AGI, the industry has to build both the brain and the body. The brain needs data that wasnât collected. The body needs someone doing the work on the ground.

That is the mission Josh, Jason and the Mecka AI team have taken on: helping physical AI labs, robotics companies and end enterprises reach physical AGI and put it to use, by being their partner for training data, reinforcement learning, and deployment.

Delivering on this mission requires developing several muscles across disciplines, all at once and all at scale:.

Research: Identify the next wave in robotics, and what it will require, before it arrives.

Hardware: Once you see the wave, design the bespoke hardware and wearables to capture the data, then manufacture them fast, economically, and at scale.

Sources indicate that operations: Run large-scale global operations to collect the data. Volume alone is not enough; the data has to span every job in every industry.

Software and digital AI: Turn the raw output, which is far more voluminous and complex than text (e.g., multi-camera video, body and hand tracking, sensor streams), into high-quality, training-ready data.

Deployment: Put robots in front of end customers, for reinforcement learning and production deployment.

In a recent development, each of these muscles is difficult to develop on its own, but to win, you need not one but all of them, working together and at scale. Training data today, for example, has to be high volume AND high diversity AND high quality AND delivered fast AND at a good price. It is easy to do one of these at small volume, but it is incredibly difficult to do all of them at once and at scale, and that is what it takes to help partners reach physical AGI. In the same way, it is easy to start a food delivery business that delivers a single dish from one restaurant to one apartment block, but it is incredibly difficult to scale it into a DoorDash.

Mecka's founders and team understood this and moved fast to build all five muscles, finding differentiated edge in each and executing on it. The result is a strong, scalable and flexible platform that has enabled them to win over many of the leading AI labs and robotics companies and quickly become the emerging leader of this category.

What drew us to Mecka is not that they made the right bet on the right form of data (although they did). Robotics is still early relative to digital AI. The form factor of the data might change. The form factor of the robots might change. What matters is that they built the machine that scales with the industry and its partners; regardless of how the input changes over time, the output will be what their partners want. In the same way, DoorDash built a system where, whether the input is a pizza or a laptop, the customer gets the same delightful delivery experience. And when something in the physical world has high barriers to scale, it is an opportunity for the right team to build a large, durable business with moats.

That is why we are excited to back Josh, Jason and their fast-growing team. We see in them the special ingredients that will keep compounding over the long term to win this category and help their partners advance the mission of building and deploying robots at scale around the world.

And it is why others have joined us, from strategics like NVIDIA, Samsung, Microsoft and Qualcomm to the founders and operators who scaled some of the most defining companies of their generation and excel in many of the disciplines required in Meckaâs business: Tony Xu, founder and CEO of DoorDash; Frank Slootman, former CEO of ServiceNow and Snowflake; Milan Kovac, former head of Optimus at Tesla; Christopher Payne, former President & COO of Doordash; Jonathan Chadwick, former COO and CFO of VMware and board member at Databricks; and many more.Photo by S72 Business Portraits.

Breaking: Sony’s updated turntable is an easy entry into the world of vinyl

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting.
  • Sources indicate that choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners.
  • In a recent development, since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting. Lately, I’ve noticed myself turning to Spotify less frequently, so it felt like the perfect time to start using a record player again.

Sources indicate that choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners. That’s where Sony’s latest PS-LX3BT turntable comes in.

In a recent development, since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies. Now that it has been discontinued, the PS-LX3BT emerges as its successor, keeping the same beginner-friendly approach while adding a few modern upgrades.

Sources indicate that at the moment priced at $399.99, the PS-LX3BT is designed for people who want to enjoy vinyl without getting too caught up in the technical side of things. It’s also a good option for those looking to upgrade from their first inexpensive turntable without having to learn how to set up or customize a more complicated audio system.

One of its biggest selling points is how easy it is to use. The PS-LX3BT features automatic playback, so you simply press start and the tonearm lifts, moves into position, and drops onto the first track for you. There’s no need to manually position the needle or worry about getting everything just right. It’s a small convenience, but one that makes the experience much less intimidating for newcomers.

Industry observers note that sony has also made a few welcome changes compared with its predecessor. The PS-LX3BT now uses USB-C for power and supports Qualcomm’s aptX Adaptive Bluetooth codec, allowing it to transmit audio at up to 24-bit/96kHz. It also has a traditional phono output alongside Bluetooth, so you can choose between a wired speaker setup and listening wirelessly.

Sources indicate that one slightly strange design decision, however, is the repositioning of the start, stop, and tonearm buttons. On the older model, these were placed outside the dust cover. Now they’re underneath it, meaning you’ll have to lift the cover just to press start. It’s not a huge inconvenience, but still kind of annoying.

According to recent reports, the turntable also offers USB connectivity for digitizing your vinyl collection. Connect it to a computer, and you can convert your records into digital audio files, which is useful if you want to preserve older records or listen to your collection on the go.

My biggest disappointment is the lack of a built-in speaker. It would have been nice to have everything included for someone just getting started. You’ll need to buy speakers (and possibly an amplifier) or compatible Bluetooth headphones separately, so keep that added cost in mind.

Industry observers note that if you’re searching for a more affordable and beginner-friendly automatic record player, there are cheaper options, such as this $179 option from Audio-Technica. But overall, Sony’s PS-LX3BT is a solid choice for anyone ready to dive into the world of vinyl for the first time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if machine intelligence were as dependable as a database query?

What if machine intelligence were as dependable as a database query?

If models have reached superhuman intelligence, where is all the automation?

Recent findings suggest that the ChatGPT moment put AI front and center in the consumer mind. Claude Code transformed the life of the individual developer. With the âJev moment,â TypeSafe is going after the next paradigm: models that power software at runtime, making zillions of decisions with no humans in the loop.

Recent findings suggest that the early response has been extraordinary. Within 24 hours of launch on September 15, TypeSafeâs first model, Jev, became the fastest-adopted model in Vercelâs AI Gateway history. Over the past few weeks, weâve heard from many of our portfolio companies, who are racing to put it into production for a myriad of fresh use cases. It is the type of developer pull we havenât seen since GPT-3.

In a recent development, jev flips the LLM on its head. Rather than writing out an answer word by word, it takes in context and a set of questions and returns typed answers with confidence scores, all at once. If LLMs are AIâs System 2, slow and deliberate, Jev is System 1: cheap, fast, intuitive and built for the thousands of small judgment calls software makes every second.

Thereâs so much you can do with Jev. Decide which button an agent should click next. Grade evals, route requests, triage tickets, pull fields out of contracts. Jev offers the kind of out-of-the-box generality that feels like magic, with no labeled data or training team required. Developers are finding new use cases every day, from playing Doom, to re-ranking their news feeds, to generating Super Mario multiverses.

Recent findings suggest that jev is named after Jevons paradox: when something gets dramatically cheaper, we use far more of it. TypeSafe is betting the same will be true of intelligence.

When classification is expensive, teams ration it. They grade a sample of agent runs rather than all of them, define brittle rules instead of calling on a model, or ask one broad question instead of ten specific ones. When classification is nearly free, those tradeoffs go away.

Industry observers note that that changes what is worth building. Many of the world's problems are Jev-shaped, which is obvious from the explosion of volume and creativity in use cases that folks are discovering. We think itâs likely that the most notable things to be built on Jev havenât even been imagined yet.

Diogo Almeida first got the idea for TypeSafe while working on InstructGPT and RLHF at OpenAI. Models were being trained to be wonderful conversational partners â great for human interaction and human-in-the-loop. But, real automation needed something different: AI that is reliable, fast, and cheap. His conclusion, which he calls the âbitterest lesson,â was that picking the right task to solve matters even more than scale.

Born in the Philippines and a *top 30* North American League of Legends player, Diogo is a rare mix: an iconoclastic, creative researcher with real developer taste and commercial instinct. He is wildly ambitious and refreshingly pragmatic, which is exactly what is needed to usher in the next machine age.

In a recent development, jev has captured lightning in a bottle, but it is only the opening salvo. TypeSafe wants to become the infrastructure layer for how software makes decisions: a platform of primitives developers can compose and build on, the way they once built on databases.

We are absolutely thrilled to be partnering with Diogo, co-founders Sasha Sheng and Erik Spock Gafni, and the TypeSafe team in their Series A, behind our friends at a16z.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI industry is entering a newly introduced era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.

Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.

“Jensen took one of the earliest major bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”.

OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.

Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”.

“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible manufacturer,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”.

It has been revealed that huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives stated during the organization’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.

Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”.

Industry observers note that “I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman noted. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”.

Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives.
  • “One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI.
  • The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The Latest York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.

“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” remarked Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman.

The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.

Sources indicate that altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.

“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman stated.

Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are right now done.

“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new … technology,” he said.

Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.

“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.

It has been revealed that openAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face. In Wednesday’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.

But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.

“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now … in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that skydance CEO David Ellison claims HBO will air Alex Gibney’s documentary about Elon Musk, even after news broke that the SpaceX founder had invested $1 billion in the newly formed company following its Warner Bro. Discovery and Paramount merger.

Following news of that investment, questions emerged over how Musk’s sizable stake in the company might affect Skydance’s plans to distribute a documentary that is highly critical of him.

When asked by The New York Times editor and columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin whether HBO would still distribute the documentary even with Musk’s stake in its parent tech giant, Ellison said, “We have a pay-one deal with A24, who produced that movie. Of course, we’re going to honor the deal.”.

He went on to say, “We believe in independence. We don’t believe in censorship of any kind.”.

Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with bringing together two major streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max, along with a portfolio of networks, including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network, under a single corporate umbrella.

More banks say customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.
  • AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.
  • But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.

AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.

But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.

Industry observers note that “As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”.

In a recent development, JPMorgan and Bank of America, the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today.

Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch.

As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a upcoming trust challenge.

Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it released earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”.

In a recent development, beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an key way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.

The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service, and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

Google’s AI feature in Search gets its own incognito mode

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (429 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account.
  • Recent findings suggest that many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included.
  • Recent findings suggest that google states that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account. Now, Google’s AI Mode in Search is getting a similar feature. In a blog post, the manufacturer unveiled a new feature that brings “temporary threads” to AI Mode, where the conversations you have won’t be resurfaced later in areas like your search history or recommendations.

Recent findings suggest that many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included. However, there was not yet an option to have a temporary chat when you’re searching Google and are dropped into its conversational interface, known as AI Mode.

Recent findings suggest that google states that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option. Instead, they’ll be able to click a temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode to engage in a temporary chat. This essentially works the same as a temporary chat would in the stand-alone Gemini chatbot.

The option could be convenient to use at those times when you start digging deeper into a particular topic via AI Mode and realize that you don’t want the discussion to become a part of your search history because of its personal nature.

Once the temporary thread is started, the session becomes detached from your account, Google says. This means that the responses the AI provides won’t be informed by past preferences, nor will they impact future personalization. That could also be useful for those times when you want to learn about something as more of a one-off, but don’t want Google to start to think of the topic as one of your main interests.

When you close out of the thread, you will return to searching as usual.

The company notes the option to engage in temporary chats in AI Mode is rolling out globally on desktop and mobile across all supported languages.

Recent findings suggest that U.K.-based fintech Payhawk confirmed a $280 million Series C funding round Wednesday, led by Goldman Sachs’ growth equity arm, making it one of Europe’s largest Series C rounds this year, as noted by Sifted. The round values the firm at $2 billion, bringing its total funding to more than $500 million to date.

Founded in 2018, Payhawk is an enterprise financial management platform that helps companies track and manage expenses and procurement using AI agents. Speaking to FinTech magazine, Payhawk’s co-founder and CEO, Hristo Borisov, said the company saw “an incredible growth opportunity and room to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payment infrastructure, and enterprise controls.”.

In a recent development, payhawk competes with spend management companies Pleo, Moss, and Spendesk, and says it operates in 33 countries. Notably, the organization remarked it still has 70% of the $100 million it raised in 2022, a round that valued the company at $1 billion. This fresh capital will support its global expansion. Other investors in the round include Greenoaks, Lightspeed, and QED.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

Software development has a new bottleneck. Writing code is no longer the hard part; trusting it is. Coding agents now produce more code than any team can read or any existing system can verify. Led by co-founders Aditya Jayaprakash (JP), Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith is building infrastructure that can.

Industry observers note that last month, Anthropicâs engineering team described what happened as their own usage of coding agents scaled. Engineers began shipping roughly eight times as much code per quarter. Their test suite grew tenfold. The volume of continuous integration (CI) jobs, the builds and tests that check every change before it reaches production, grew 25x in six months. Anthropic is very far along the curve, but is on the same curve as every company, and its advice to the rest of the industry was to plan for 25x the CI load within two quarters.

For decades, software development scaled as a function of engineering capacity. Developers were the scarce resource. Shipping more meant hiring more. That has changed. Developers now direct fleets of coding agents that work in parallel, around the clock and increasingly autonomously. These agents do not produce finished work. They produce attemptsâa patch, a test, a migration, a throwaway branchâeach iterating against a test suite until it is ready to merge. Meanwhile, the quiet backbone of software development that validates and tests code has not changed.

Validating code has also never been more key. AI coding tasks produce large volumes of security flaws, and the same model capabilities that write the code now make those flaws more dangerous. The system that was supposed to catch them is straining right as developers need it the most. With the scale and velocity of this shift, the constraint in software has moved from writing code to proving it works and is safe.

It has been revealed that this is the problem Blacksmith set out to solve. The team started with speeding up CI. With a one-line change in a workflow file, developers using Blacksmith see their CI jobs complete twice as fast and at 60% lower cost on average. Underneath a simple product experience is a stack purpose-built from the bare metal up, designed to absorb demand spikes from customers and get faster and more efficient as it scales.

Developers have noticed. The business has seen explosive growth this year. More than 10,000 companies are using Blacksmith, up from 700 a year ago. Weekly CI jobs are up 18x, from 5 million to 90 million, in 2026 alone. And ARR has grown 17x over the same time period, with the largest customers now spending more than $1M per year.

Recent findings suggest that much of our conviction in Blacksmith is driven by the team behind it. Co-founders JP, Aayush and Maru have known each other since their undergraduate years at the University of Waterloo, and developed a maniacal focus on hyper-performant systems at Cockroach Labs and Faire. They founded Blacksmith in 2024, as autocomplete was giving way to coding assistants, on the conviction that the volume of code needing to be tested would go up by orders of magnitude. For the rest of the world, the future became clear in 2026 with the arrival of truly autonomous coding agents, but Blacksmith had already been building for it. The Blacksmith team is talent-dense and is growing quickly. The roadmap is exciting, with several launches planned in the coming months.

Sources indicate that we are proud to lead Blacksmithâs Series C. The world is about to run far more code than it has ever written, and someone has to make sure it works. We look forward to supporting JP, Aayush and Maru as they build infrastructure that runs at agent speed, in validation and beyond.

  • In a recent development, the tech giant is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile.
  • The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snapchat declared on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.

In a recent development, the tech giant is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.

The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the tech giant is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.

In a recent development, developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat states it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.

It has been revealed that lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.

With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.

It has been revealed that AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat claims.

The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The organization notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.

Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
