Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.

“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.

As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.

In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023.

According to recent reports, “If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said onstage at the Fresh York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.”.

Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.).

So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life?

In a recent development, “The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman noted. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.”.

Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted.

Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.”.

“It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.”.

Zuckerberg mentioned he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a organization outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him.

Sources indicate that zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir.

Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays.

According to recent reports, “I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a manufacturer or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”.

Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey thinks Nvidia’s board is giving China exactly what it wants by removing the company’s longtime CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang.

It has been revealed that nvidia, the leading semiconductor designer whose chips power much of the AI industry, is undergoing a critical, unexpected leadership change. Huang, who led the company for 33 years, stepped down last week amid several controversies, including his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy who has been investigated for possibly smuggling Nvidia chips into China to circumvent U.S. export restrictions.

Sources indicate that “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey noted onstage at The Latest York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, repeating a statement he posted on X last week. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.”.

Industry observers note that luckey disagrees with Huang’s longstanding position that Nvidia should have more leeway to export chips to China. But he also recognizes that China stands to benefit if its domestic chipmakers can challenge Nvidia’s dominance.

“China doesn’t want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies,” Luckey said. “There are Chinese companies that want to buy Nvidia GPUs… China will not give them an import permit because they want to build an internal domestic processor industry… not build one that is dependent on the United States.”.

Industry observers note that nvidia has remarked as much itself — the U.S. government granted the organization license to ship some of its powerful H200 chips to certain Chinese customers, but those sales were restricted by the Chinese government. Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that it will no longer sell H200 chips in China at all.

Luckey is far from alone among industry peers in his defense of Huang.

Industry observers note that more than 200,000 people — including Elon Musk and the CEOs of Y Combinator, Databricks, Epic Games, Shopify, and Replit — have signed a petition calling for Nvidia to reinstate its founder. But Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that the company does not have aims to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them, Palmer Luckey warned at The Upcoming York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are struggling to keep pace with the new hacking capabilities enabled by AI and warned it was time to quicken the pace of securing our defenses.

“We’re seeing the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools allowing for the creation of various exploits,” he remarked.

While government officials largely attributed the latest set of technical challenges to companies rushing to patch their systems to protect against the new vulnerabilities AI has discovered, Luckey focused on the underlying security challenges facing organizations using outdated technology.

Industry observers note that luckey explained that U.S. adversaries are currently exploiting the mismatch between latest attack capabilities and our defense capabilities. These attacks are being carried out for both strategic and financial reasons, and North Korea was particularly involved, he added.

The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, noted that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance had canceled his appearance at the Times’ conference this week because of the recent tech outages, saying he now had to attend meetings about the matter.

Given the situation, Sorkin asked Luckey how worried we should be about all this.

Recent findings suggest that “It depends on how well prepared you are,” was Luckey’s answer. (He then ominously warned, “You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough.”).

The tech executive argued that AI could ultimately give defenders the upper hand, but they’d have to move more promptly.

According to recent reports, “In the long run, the advantages are going to accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense,” Luckey said. “With the people who say that everything can be hacked — they are right, for now. That actually may be the case with certain new techniques that are coming along. But as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers who are very fast-moving and using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” Luckey continued.

“And I think … people are going to have to pick up the pace,” he said. “It’s time to start running.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that during Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She stated Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC.
  • According to recent reports, the delay was widely noticed.
  • The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that during Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She stated Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.

According to recent reports, the delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.

The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.

The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.

It has been revealed that “The company revealed that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).

Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the manufacturer’s disclosures misled investors.

It has been revealed that so the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.).

Recent findings suggest that the delay suggests the organization may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.

Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.

There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Defense mogul Palmer Luckey — whose $90 billion drone and weapons startup Anduril is flush with government contracts — is still the kind of guy who prepares for the worst.

During Luckey’s conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the billionaire implied that Americans should batten down the hatches in case there are rough times ahead. Luckey himself has taken steps to prepare for a potential cataclysmic event, he noted.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a series of recent large-scale outages — at Apple, at Microsoft, at the NSA, and at the Federal Aviation Administration — that have led to concerns that America may be under attack by cyberthreat actors. The government has said that this is not the case, but Luckey cryptically teased that there may be more to the story.

“Look, all the 4chan schizo posters are like 12 hours ahead of the mainstream media on this. You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough,” he said.

Sorkin also asked Luckey to expound on comments made backstage “about what might be a cyber war that seems to be going on around us.”.

According to recent reports, luckey described a “mismatch” between the sophisticated AI-powered cyberattacks that exist today and “old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as swiftly as it is developed.” He added: “I think people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.”.

It has been revealed that “What does that mean? Are you a prepper?” Sorkin asked.

Luckey didn’t deny the characterization. “I own a missile base 200 feet underground,” he answered, to audience laughter. “It’s a funny joke, but a missile base is actually a pretty bad way to run from the apocalypse. Everyone knows exactly where you are, and they [bases] are designed to take a hit from a nuclear weapon, a blast overpressure event.”.

However, he had some qualifications on the prepper label. “The point is, like everyone should have three days of water. Everyone should have three days of dry food. If you have prescription medication, don’t go refill it when you run out. Make sure you refill it 72 hours before you run out.”.

“People used to be taught this in middle school, and now everyone who remembers that is treated like a nut,” he added.

It has been revealed that it should be pointed out that preparing for the apocalypse is not necessarily a new interest for Luckey. In 2017, a person familiar with the billionaire described him as a “prepper” and the bunker that was broached Wednesday is one of several decommissioned Cold War era underground bases that Luckey has purchased over the years. In 2024, he revealed that his massive video game collection is housed in one of them.

Partnering with Edelbyte: Data Infrastructure That Keeps Up With AI's Curiosity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents will ask far more questions of a organization's data than people ever did.
  • According to recent reports, AI agents will ask far more questions of a company's data than people ever did.
  • In a recent development, last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents will ask far more questions of a organization's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

According to recent reports, AI agents will ask far more questions of a company's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

In a recent development, last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft. This was the only introduction to a founding team weâd ever received from Roy, and we paid attention.

Recent findings suggest that the people Roy wanted us to meet had built Kusto, a data engine that started more than a decade ago as a small incubation project inside Microsoft. Named after the oceanographer Jacques Cousteau because it was built for diving into oceans of data, Kusto was designed to get answers from enormous volumes of fast-arriving data, such as logs, telemetry and security events, in seconds rather than hours. It ran on a query language simple enough that anyone, not just massive-data engineers, could use it. And it worked so well that it became the data engine underneath Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor, and was eventually offered to customers as Azure Data Explorer. Security teams in particular loved it, which is how Roy became one of its biggest champions. When we spoke with customers, large enterprises and fast-growing startups alike told us two things: it was game-changing data technology, and the team behind it was among the best theyâd ever worked with.

Avner Aharoni, Evgeney Ryzhyk, Alexander Sloutsky and Yoni Leibowitz were that team. Evgeney invented the Kusto engine and its query language, then rebuilt it three times, making it faster and cheaper with each iteration. Alexander turned half-formed ideas into finished features seemingly overnight, and Yoni made sure every complex design was fully thought through, starting before a line of code was ever written. Avner, who spent a quarter century at Microsoft, hustled Kusto from project to a globally beloved product. Their new tech giant, Edelbyte, builds on this success. We are proud to have led their seed round and to be their partners.

Industry observers note that in B2B technology, this is a proven playbook: a team develops a solution inside a large company and then splits off to build it independently. Itâs the origin story of Sequoia portfolio companies such as Confluent, whose founders created Kafka at LinkedIn, and Temporal, whose founders built Cadence at Uber. Edelbyte now follows the same path.

But Edelbyte is not simply Kusto rebuilt for a fourth time; it is a rethinking, from first principles, of what a data platform should look like in the age of AI. With every major shift in computing, the way software is built changes, and the data infrastructure underneath it has to change too. Data platforms were designed around human owners, and there is a natural limit on the number of questions one person can type in a day. That made the trade-offs, such as keeping less history so queries stay fast, asking fewer questions so the bill stays reasonable, and building the product inside whichever cloud the database happens to run in, easier to tolerate.

In a recent development, but an AI agent investigating a problem is like a whole team of curious analysts who never get tired, testing multiple hypotheses concurrently. One agent might fire off fifty queries where a person would run one. And at that scale, rationing and trade-offs promptly constrain the true promise of AI. An agent is only as useful as the questions it can afford to ask, and what it can afford is decided in the data layer.

Edelbyte keeps detailed history queryable at interactive speed, scales as data volumes and query demand grow, and gives people, applications and AI agents governed access to the same data. It brings search and analytics, which have historically been stitched together from separate systems at significant cost and complexity, together in a single platform. And it runs wherever you need it: in the cloud or on premises, managed or self-hosted.

The result is exactly what an AI-heavy workload needs: no more rationing curiosity, whether it comes from a person or an agent. Already, customers are seeing dramatic increases in efficiency, including tenfold increases in queries with no increase in budget.

Data platforms are among the most durable and lucrative businesses in technology, because data has gravity; once it accumulates in one place it rarely moves. Each era produces its own winners, and we believe the AI era will be won by the platform that lets builders, and the agents working for them, ask as many questions as they want without worrying about the speed or the bill. Edelbyte is building just such a platform, and we are thrilled to be part of the journey.

  • At the IPO price, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that anthropic has priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry. The Claude maker sold 980 million shares in the offering, up from the 825 million initially planned, generating $81.3 billion in proceeds and surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion record to become the largest IPO in history by proceeds raised.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public firm on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

The firm’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce prepares for an IPO.

According to recent reports, although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the manufacturer, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers. Investors who own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia, as well as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm introduced by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher. Spark Capital, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company (it was the first institutional investor in the company, leading its $450 million Series C round in 2023 that valued the company at $4.5 billion), also stands to make a fortune off its early investment in Anthropic.

Some of the Anthropic’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they are reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the manufacturer’s shares in the IPO.

Sources indicate that yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the company’s strategic partners Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

The company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.

This post has been updated with the number of shares sold and IPO proceeds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic.
  • Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago.
  • Sources indicate that “The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” stated Nadella.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic.

Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago.

Sources indicate that “The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” stated Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC [cost-per-click] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.”.

Recent findings suggest that the discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage.

Industry observers note that “I think this is going to be interesting,” he stated, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? Which is, if you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said.

  • During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.

It has been revealed that “Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”.

In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.

Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”.

“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.

It has been revealed that “Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”.

Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.

Sources indicate that “We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.

“The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”.

Elon Musk says: ‘I’m not MAGA’

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk, who spent $277 million to get Donald Trump reelected president in 2024 and who, during that campaign, declared himself “dark MAGA” and who, after the election, was subsequently photographed sporting a cartoonishly large MAGA hat while visiting the Oval Office, has some news for Americans: None of that necessarily makes him MAGA.
  • Recent findings suggest that “I’m not MAGA,” Musk declared Wednesday during a conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times DealBook Summit.
  • “Well, at least I’m not like … I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he backtracked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk, who spent $277 million to get Donald Trump reelected president in 2024 and who, during that campaign, declared himself “dark MAGA” and who, after the election, was subsequently photographed sporting a cartoonishly large MAGA hat while visiting the Oval Office, has some news for Americans: None of that necessarily makes him MAGA.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not MAGA,” Musk declared Wednesday during a conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times DealBook Summit. Musk joined the conversation via video call, as he is currently in China, joining President Trump for the APEC summit.

“Well, at least I’m not like … I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he backtracked. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”.

According to recent reports, the comments were made amidst a broader question about how Musk felt in the wake of this year’s midterms, during which a “blue wave” led to Democratic victories throughout the country. Musk, notably, spent a gargantuan amount of money (reportedly some $445 million) to support Republican candidates. Musk admitted Wednesday that such vast political spending might not have been a good use of his money.

Industry observers note that “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seen much for it,” he stated. “Or maybe it would have been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that, you know, American elections are not just about money.”.

Recent findings suggest that during his conversation with Sorkin, Musk also seemed to lean away from his viral edgelord persona and claimed that he held no extreme views. He said: “I don’t think I have like, you know, any kind of extreme political views.”.

Sorkin pushed Musk on this a little, noting that some people found his views on immigration extreme, to which Musk said: “Like what?” Mild laughter spread throughout the audience.

In a recent development, ironically, the last time Musk spoke at DealBook, in 2023, he was in the middle of a very public battle with his social media site X’s advertisers. Critics had accused Musk of platforming a typhoon of hateful content on his site, and advertisers were threatening to walk over it. In response, Musk famously told Sorkin that he hoped those advertisers would “go f—” themselves.

Recent findings suggest that now Musk has an entirely fresh set of concerns. Democratic lawmakers in various committees have signaled that they may investigate Musk and his business activities as they probe potential corruption throughout the Trump administration.

Specifically, officials have stated they’re interested in scrutinizing Musk’s role in DOGE, the “government efficiency” initiative that Musk launched inside the White House at the start of Trump’s new term, as well as Starlink’s activities in Ukraine, where the manufacturer has been accused of throttling the military’s access to its internet service.

Sorkin broached some of the potential concerns for the Tesla CEO: “You hear people like the chairman of the oversight committee saying, ‘Lawyer up,’ and you hear the president saying, ‘If I have to give him a pardon’ — meaning you — ‘I’ll give him a pardon.’”.

Musk replied: “I don’t think I need a pardon by the way, because I haven’t committed any crimes.”.

Musk then made one of those controversial statements he’s known for, appearing to compare an incoming Texas official to Lavrentiy Beria, the top head of the Soviet secret police under Josef Stalin.

“The incoming Texas, you know, House Majority Leader, said that I should go to prison,” Musk said. “I’m like, the guy’s trying to, you know channel Beria from, like, Stalin, where it’s, you know, show me the man, I’ll show you the crime type of thing.”.

It’s not clear who (or what) Musk was talking about. Texas doesn’t have a House Majority Leader. However, he may have been referencing Gene Wu, who is the incoming chair of the Texas House Democratic caucus and who has suggested that Musk be investigated for potential criminal activity.

“Hopefully, in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison,” Musk added.

#7311. Tech Report: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (634 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.
  • Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect.
  • The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.

Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.

The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.

Industry observers note that “Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained.

For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.”.

He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.”.

He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.”.

But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’”.

When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.”.

In a recent development, he called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.”.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the fresh AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.

#7299. Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming.
  • Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.
  • Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.

Industry observers note that organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

Recent findings suggest that LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

With these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously mentioned the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard.

According to recent reports, free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

This might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

Sources indicate that while direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team mentioned in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”.

Recent findings suggest that LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

Usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Also: Can you still trust Proton?

In a recent development, organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.
  • The upcoming remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is testing a newly introduced feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.

The upcoming remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

Once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the new feature allows IT admins to respond promptly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up.

It has been revealed that the remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Microsoft blames major outage on a July enhancement defect – and two other factors

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft has released upcoming information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.
  • Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July update to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.
  • Recent findings suggest that “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft has released upcoming information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July update to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Low server capacity and peak traffic in the US brought the defect out of hiding, despite no prior reported issues.

Recent findings suggest that “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable,” Lamanna mentioned, noting that the update was deployed safely worldwide without any issues for over three months.

He noted Microsoft didn’t find the issue in testing due to “the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” because “our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.”.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited.

Two other factors made matters worse, and left servers useless in less than two hours.

Sources indicate that “A surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention,” Lamanna remarked, explaining that Microsoft 365 maintains two gateway systems. Before the outage started, Teams failed from one to the other, which “changed its traffic patterns.” Simultaneously, he added, “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated matter from the previous day.”.

Industry observers note that those two conditions collided and “caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna concluded. Requests eventually overloaded servers, at which point they stopped responding. At the outage’s low point, over 80% of its servers weren’t responding.

According to recent reports, “When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route owners to other healthy endpoints,” Lamanna stated. “However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers.”.

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in.

Before Microsoft issued an explanation, some suspected the outage may have been the result of a cyberattack, which both Lamanna and Microsoft’s status account denied.

Recent findings suggest that it’s unclear how many people the outage affected, though Microsoft’s own numbers from January say Microsoft 365 “exceeds 450 million commercial paid seats,” illustrating the scale of the matter. Microsoft deployed an revision to fix the outage and gradually applied it to groups of servers. Lamanna noted Microsoft would publish a full post-incident review with more details later this week.

Service might be restored, but customers aren’t happy about having lost nearly two full workdays. One think tank told CNN it estimated the outage — which lasted through close of business on Friday for some — resulted in $7 billion in losses, due to many businesses and organizations being unable to access their everyday systems.

Also: If the November Windows enhancement fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do.

The fact that Microsoft’s testing couldn’t find the July issue ahead of time may leave customers wondering when the next dormant defect will strike, and whether the tech giant is prepared.

Organizations across Europe have been leaving Microsoft in recent years, opting instead for locally-controlled, open-source alternatives. The former CEO of Github debuted a decentralized alternative called Entire earlier this year, citing developers’ need for something more reliable, as Github has similarly been plagued with outages.

For many, Teams was barely offline over the two-day period, or was the first service to come back online.

According to recent reports, “Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without glitch for most of the outage,” Lamanna explained. Other services like Exchange Online can’t fail out.

He added that fixing the outage was slow because waiting traffic hit servers as soon as they came back, rendering them unresponsive just as swiftly.

It has been revealed that “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state,” Lamanna stated. “Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to rapidly revert the change.”.

It has been revealed that on Thursday morning, people began reporting problems with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Also: If the November Windows revision fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do.

As late as Friday afternoon, the company didn’t yet have an ETA of when the outage would be fully solved.

In a recent development, although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

It has been revealed that iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its upcoming smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a newly introduced button.

Recent findings suggest that the report indicates that many consumers don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

In a recent development, apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give owners greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

Technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Industry observers note that apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower.

For many customers, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Industry observers note that gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

Sources indicate that CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended.

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

Because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

#7282. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1164 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities.
  • Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?
  • The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the newly introduced reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s upcoming security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”.

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target.

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’.

However, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

Sources indicate that A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

According to recent reports, threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

Industry observers note that bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

In a recent development, as a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are.

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security problems introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against latest and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

According to recent reports, single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance.

Industry observers note that CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it released the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Industry observers note that apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, remarked in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for.

Participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

Sources indicate that apple often debuts studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now.

Industry observers note that the AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which launches officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google launched its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

Sources indicate that A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

It has been revealed that “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this upcoming health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

Industry observers note that if you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.

#7278. We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (979 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some, a tablet is a lightweight e-reader, or a more portable way to browse the web, take notes, and stream movies.
  • Industry observers note that rugged tablets differ from regular tablets in that they are usually military-grade certified for durability and can operate in more extreme temperatures.
  • Industry observers note that ZDNET’s lab in Louisville, KY, tested seven tablets from brands like Samsung, Dell, and more, by putting them in frigid-cold and sweltering-hot conditions to see how their battery life would hold up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some, a tablet is a lightweight e-reader, or a more portable way to browse the web, take notes, and stream movies. For others, a tablet is a capable and durable device that needs to withstand outdoor conditions like fieldwork, camping, or construction sites. In these instances, you’ll need a rugged tablet.

Also: The best rugged tablets you can buy.

Industry observers note that rugged tablets differ from regular tablets in that they are usually military-grade certified for durability and can operate in more extreme temperatures. Since their build and intent are different from regular tablets, we decided to develop a upcoming test to compare rugged tablets and their performance capabilities.

Industry observers note that ZDNET’s lab in Louisville, KY, tested seven tablets from brands like Samsung, Dell, and more, by putting them in frigid-cold and sweltering-hot conditions to see how their battery life would hold up. Based on our extensive testing, the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro won our cold test, and the Oukitel RT10 won our hot test.

To test these tablets, we first needed to test their baseline battery life. Gianmarco Chumbe, our lab’s product testing manager, battery-tested these tablets at room temperature (72°F) with the following configurations: screens set to ~500 nits of brightness, Airplane Mode on, a looped playback of the same 1080p H.264 video file (no audio track) in VLC, and the system audio muted. Each tablet started out at 100% battery.

Recent findings suggest that to document battery degradation, a lightweight Python script ran on each tablet throughout the test and logged the battery level every minute. For Windows tablets — like the Dell Pro Rugged models — it read the battery status via the psutil library. Android tablets like the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro used the Termux app to read the battery status via the Termux API. Each tablet plays the looped video, with logging running, until playback stops. We found that Windows tablets were set to shut down at their critical battery level, and Android tablets entered a dormant state at about 1%.

After getting the baseline results above, Chumbe focused on our cold test, which consisted of placing each tablet in a consumer freezer set to -6°F and running the same configuration as above to simulate a harsh winter environment. Battery life drops were documented once per minute — the same as the baseline test.

The heat test required a more complex setup: Chumbe created a “tablet sauna” using a 40 × 20 × 20-inch enclosure with walls made of half-inch PVC board and a quarter-inch acrylic front panel for viewing the tablets during testing. A 400 Watt fan-forced PTC heater sat at one end of the chamber, while a 20 × 12-in aluminum baffle, positioned 10 inches in front of the heater, blocked its direct airflow, so no tablet was directly heated by it. A circulation fan ran continuously to keep the air evenly mixed.

Recent findings suggest that the thermostat was set between 104 and 106°F, with the heater cycling roughly every 2 minutes (30 seconds on and 90 seconds off). A second, independent thermostat cut power to the heater if the air reached 115°F, protecting the units if the main thermostat failed. Finally, a single 1 ⅛-in. port, sealed around the cables, carried the power and sensor cords. Again, the same configurations and documentation process were used.

Also: How we test tablets at ZDNET in 2026.

Some caveats to keep in mind about our testing: the test temperatures reflect the surrounding air, not the device temperature, and while every tablet ran the same video at the same measured brightness, the screen size, panel, processor, and battery capacity differ for each tablet tested. Runtimes reflect each tablet as sold and aren’t normalized for battery size.

As you can see from Fig. 1 above, the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro won our cold test, lasting 12 hours and 47 minutes at -6°F. An honorable mention goes to the Oukitel RT10, which remained at 1% battery for one hour.

Read the reviews: Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro | Oukitel RT10.

Sources indicate that an interesting result we had was that neither of the Dell Rugged Tablets completed our cold test. The Dell Pro Rugged 12 Tablet tapped out at 5.10 hours at 78% battery, and the Dell Pro Rugged 10 Tablet stopped working after 6.23 hours at 67% battery. Both tablets displayed “Extreme cold T detected, shutting down for safety.”.

In a recent development, according to Dell’s official operating manual, both tablets should be able to withstand temperatures as low as -20.2°F. Dell states in its manual that performance can be reduced once temperatures reach 5°F, but the whole point of rugged tablets is to withstand harsh elements without needing to move to a warmer area for them to work.

ZDNET reached out to Dell to comment on these results, and we will enhancement this story once they respond.

In our heat test, the tablet that lasted the longest in our tablet sauna was the Oukitel RT10, which persisted for 32.07 hours. And even though the Dell Pro Rugged tablet didn’t complete our cold test, it came in second for our heat test and lasted 21.65 hours.

Sources indicate that as you can see from both Fig. 1 and Fig. 2, the DT Research Rugged Tablet DT312RP had the worst-performing battery out of both tests; however, it wasn’t far off from its original baseline result of 4.43 hours, and even outperformed that baseline number in the heat test (4.65 hours).

According to recent reports, our test results might differ from your own experiences with these tablets, especially depending on the temperature at which you use them and the applications/connections you have running. However, as a benchmark, our testing provides real-world results on how different rugged tablets can handle extreme conditions.

Oura’s newly introduced feature could help you kick jet lag – how to enable it

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (392 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Oura developed a tool for its frequent-flying members that could help them stave off the worst of jet lag.
  • Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, on Tuesday, Oura revealed Jet Lag Proposal, a new feature designed to help travelers feel alert and energized after crossing several time zones.
  • Also: Oura Ring consumers may get in-app access to real doctors soon – what we know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oura developed a tool for its frequent-flying members that could help them stave off the worst of jet lag.

Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, on Tuesday, Oura revealed Jet Lag Proposal, a new feature designed to help travelers feel alert and energized after crossing several time zones.

Also: Oura Ring consumers may get in-app access to real doctors soon – what we know.

Jet Lag Plan takes into account your travel itinerary, sleep patterns, and body responses to provide guidance for traveling members entering newly introduced time zones.

Jet lag happens when circadian rhythms are at odds with local time zones, but there are a few things people can do to adjust.

Oura factors in the direction of travel, how many time zones are crossed, individual light windows, and sleep timing.

Ring consumers will enter their flight details, including information like multi-stop trips, and also include the reason for the trip. Oura adjusts the Jet Lag Strategy accordingly, and a business trip’s plan may differ in intensity from that of a vacation.

“Two people on the same flight can get different looks, because guidance reflects your itinerary, your typical sleep schedule, and your chronotype,” Oura writes in a blog post. The chronotype refers to Oura’s sleep chronotype, which categorizes consumers into six types (early morning, morning, early evening, and so on) based on their historical sleep activity.
